title: 28-Year-Old Running for Congress [Joby Bernstein]
guest: Peter Pham, co-founder and managing director of Science Venture Studios (incubator behind Liquid Death and Dollar Shave Club)
summary: Despite the batch title, this transcript is a short conference interview with Peter Pham of Science Venture Studios, followed by the hosts' case-study-style takeaways. Pham shares his refugee-camp-to-VC origin story, a Buddhist-inflected philosophy of dropping wanting and forgetting setbacks, and his thesis that you invest in culture by living in it, judging brands by whether the comment section treats them like customer service or like a friend. The hosts extend this to comment-led marketing, brand authenticity, leverage in management, and their own Sisters Matcha brand.

ideas.idea: Rules are a construct; reason from first principles and challenge any rule that does not make sense.
ideas.detail: Pham says media and pop culture define what things are 'supposed' to be, so he always asks why; if a rule makes sense he follows it, if not he does not mind breaking it. He was a literal rule breaker as a kid, committing crimes at 10-11 while growing up seven to a one-bedroom apartment in Santa Fe Springs and Norwalk.

ideas.idea: Remove wanting from your life: wanting means you are not happy until you get the thing, so be present and grateful instead.
ideas.detail: His advice to his 35-year-old self, framed as a Buddhist principle after a retreat with Mongolian monks; he says he already has everything he needs. The hosts note this matches the 'I have everything I need' mantra printed on their Sisters Matcha can.

ideas.idea: A terrible memory is a superpower: your future self will forget the bad thing anyway, so do not waste energy wallowing on it.
ideas.detail: Pham says nobody wants to be around you when you give off sad energy. The hosts observe a Season 3 trend of guests with deliberately short memories who move on and keep iterating.

ideas.idea: If you love what you do you will win, because you think about it 24/7 while 9-to-5 competitors stop at 5pm on Friday.
ideas.detail: You do not need to be the smartest person in the subject; loving it means it never feels like work and you naturally out-work people who treat it as a regular job. Be willing to give something up, even move in with your parents, to pay rent while you do it.

ideas.idea: People want to help those who are visibly passionate because most people never follow their own dreams and live vicariously through yours.
ideas.detail: Like tipping a street musician or wanting to help someone who says they are an artist, people see a bit of their own unlived dream in you. Jean confirms that once she started publicly sharing her passion for Sisters Matcha, people began reaching out to help.

ideas.idea: Supporting other people's wins lets you feel like you are winning every day, the same psychology that keeps sports fans loyal.
ideas.detail: Pham says his happiness is driven by other people's success, which makes venture incubation the perfect job for him; COVID was terrible because he could not be around people. The hosts connect this to why customers want to feel part of a founder's story.

ideas.idea: Depression is a luxury of time that Americans have; most of the world is too busy with war, famine and where to eat.
ideas.detail: Pham relays a Buddhist monk's observation and says having grown from nothing and travelling to see poverty gives him gratitude, e.g. noticing they are sitting in a five-star hotel.

ideas.idea: To invest in culture you must participate in culture: get off the coasts, travel the Midwest, and reset your social feeds to see how everyone else lives.
ideas.detail: He rarely visits a city twice, was just in Nebraska, and says if you only watch LA and New York you have no idea what is happening in the world. He recommends resetting TikTok and Instagram feeds and searching for unfamiliar things so the algorithm shows you other people's worlds.

ideas.idea: Each platform has a job: X for real-time information, Instagram for specific demographics like music culture, TikTok and YouTube as television, Reddit for deep obsessive information.
ideas.detail: Pham calls himself chronically online by necessity and spends his time reading comments; the hosts agree that YouTube is television and creators are the new brands.

ideas.idea: The test of a durable brand is whether people in its comment section treat it like customer service or like a friend, because relationships last longer than customer support.
ideas.detail: On Liquid Death's TikTok and Instagram, fans joke with the brand and defend it against critics; on American Airlines' pages people just complain and ask for DMs. Pham told investors that day that this is how you evaluate culture brands, and says Liquid Death's community was built by design.

ideas.idea: Consumers are smarter than you think and know they are being marketed to, so treat the audience like they are in on the joke.
ideas.detail: At Dollar Shave Club and Liquid Death the stance is 'we know that they know that we know'. Pick a position, own it and do not waver, because someone will hit you and if you flinch you get destroyed.

ideas.idea: Two to four percent of any population just loves to hate; haters are the high-school instigators at scale and you should ignore them rather than fuel them.
ideas.detail: Pham says people are 100 times more likely to respond to a hate comment, which is exactly what instigators want; human nature does not change, which is why he loves investing in culture. Cherie adds that haters actually love you most because they follow you obsessively.

ideas.idea: We live in a post-truth, algorithm-fragmented world, so there will never be another Madonna or Michael Jackson-scale monoculture star.
ideas.detail: Everyone's algorithm is different: nobody knew the number-one song, a friend had never heard Diet Pepsi or Bed Chem, and people now listen to 100+ artists and single songs instead of 10-15 artists and full albums. The remaining mega-artists like Taylor Swift built their base pre-Spotify.

ideas.idea: Conferences are about people, not panels: the value compounds when you show up consistently and turn two-minute hellos into 20-minute conversations year after year.
ideas.detail: Having attended tech conferences for 20 years since TechCrunch launched in Mike Arrington's apartment, Pham says late-night bar conversations build relationships; 20 people downstairs are 15-year relationships, including showing Evan Spiegel around LA when Snapchat was young. He also mines conversations with people in big non-Silicon-Valley industries, like the largest mini-storage owner or NIL athlete manager, for business ideas.

ideas.idea: Coming from nothing makes you unafraid and makes it easier to take big career risks, because you know the worst case is survivable.
ideas.detail: Cherie links Pham's refugee background to the Vu Tran episode and says peers afraid to leave corporate 9-to-5s have not actually run the worst-case analysis, e.g. moving in with family to save money, which requires living below your means and sacrifice.

ideas.idea: Define a North Star you genuinely love thinking about and every decision compounds toward it, as Kim Kardashian did with fame.
ideas.detail: Jean recalls home videos of Kardashian at 16-17 saying she would be famous; her politics involvement and PE/investment fund all expand the total addressable market for her name. Loving money can be a legitimate motivator in the same way.

ideas.idea: Comment-led marketing works only for brands that are 'comment native' and authentic; copying Duolingo's snark does not work for Ryanair, Spirit or Quaker Oats.
ideas.detail: The hosts predict a comment-led marketing playbook within two years and praise Duolingo's Gen Z social manager, but say budget airlines are only halfway there: to be truly in on the joke they would own how bad they are and repost passengers wearing all their clothes. Quaker Oats should start from first principles, e.g. recipe content, rather than snark.

ideas.idea: Deeply understanding people and culture is how you create something out of nothing, like turning commodity water into a hardcore brand.
ideas.detail: Jean recalls HBS marketing professor Youngme Moon assigning students to invent a branded water because water is a commodity; Liquid Death later proved there is room for 30+ water brands by creating a culture around canned water.

ideas.idea: As you move into senior management, the number-one skill is increasing your leverage so one action kicks off ten workstreams that reach thousands of people.
ideas.detail: Jean says this was the top feedback she received as a middle manager moving up at a social media app used by hundreds of millions; it is the corporate version of Pham's 'win every day through other people'.

ideas.idea: Make customers feel part of the story: the hosts write every Sisters Matcha buyer's name on their office wall so customers appear in their videos.
ideas.detail: People want to feel they contributed 1-10% to a win; the wall plus the story of the small family farm in Wazuka, Japan, differentiates their matcha the way heritage lets a handmade Hermes bag command $6,000-$150,000 versus $150 for another handmade French bag.

ideas.idea: Growth and retention depend on shortening the time to the customer's 'aha moment', and the challenge is delivering that moment at scale.
ideas.detail: Cherie borrows the concept from her LinkedIn onboarding work; for matcha the aha moment is standing on the farm hearing head farmer Daiki-san's story, which few can do, so the hosts plan a documentary and a May 2025 group trip to Japan with 15 spots.
